lines.text: An island of mountains off the coast of China, ruled in turn by Dutch, Qing, Japanese and Nationalists, that made itself a democracy. This is Taiwan.
For thousands of years Austronesian peoples lived here, in villages of the plains and the mountains. Their ancestors may have spread across the Pacific.
In 1624 the Dutch built Fort Zeelandia in the south, and the island they called Formosa became a trading colony.
In 1662 Koxinga, a commander loyal to the fallen Ming, drove the Dutch out and set up a kingdom of his own.
From 1683 the Qing empire ruled the island for two centuries, while farmers from Fujian crossed the strait and settled the west.
In 1875 Taipei was made a prefecture, the start of the city that would become the island's capital.
Chiang Kai-shek, leader of China's Nationalists, would one day bring his government to Taiwan after losing the civil war.
In 1895, after losing a war, China gave the island to Japan, and for fifty years Taiwan was a Japanese colony.
In 1912 the Kuomintang, the Chinese Nationalist party, was born. It would later rule Taiwan for decades.
Lee Teng-hui, born on the island under Japanese rule, would one day lead it into democracy.
Two years after the Nationalists arrived, in February 1947, an uprising against them was crushed, and thousands were killed.
In 1949 martial law began. It lasted thirty-eight years, a time of fear remembered as the White Terror.
That year, defeated on the mainland, the government of the Republic of China moved to Taipei. Its status is disputed by Beijing to this day.
On the small island of Kinmen, in 1949, Nationalist troops stopped the Communists from crossing further.
Tsai Ing-wen would become Taiwan's first woman president, serving eight years.
Lai Ching-te, a doctor turned politician, would follow her as president in 2024.
From the sixties, factories boomed and exports soared, and Taiwan became one of the four Asian tigers.
In 1965 the National Palace Museum opened in Taipei, holding hundreds of thousands of treasures of Chinese art brought from Beijing.
On the east coast, the marble walls of Taroko Gorge became a national park in 1986.
A year later Morris Chang founded TSMC, which makes chips for other companies. Today much of the world's technology depends on it.
Martial law had ended, and in 1996 Taiwan held its first direct vote for president, even as Chinese missile tests splashed nearby.
In September 1999 a great earthquake struck central Taiwan and killed more than two thousand people.
Taipei 101 rose like a stack of boxes, the tallest building in the world for some years, steadied by a giant steel ball inside.
In 2014 students occupied the legislature to stop a trade pact with China, in what became the Sunflower Movement.
In 2019 Taiwan became the first place in Asia to allow same-sex marriage.
In April 2024 the strongest earthquake in a quarter of a century shook Hualien on the east coast.
From ancient villages to the world's most advanced chips, Taiwan has written its own story under pressure.
